title: Introduction to Azithromycin (AZM)
description: What AZM is, who receives it, how often, and how it is delivered.

content.caption: The AZM medicine bottle, as shown on the cover of the training flipbook.
content.alt: A white medicine bottle with a teal label reading AZM, inside a white circle.

content.text: Purpose of AZM training

items: Learn the knowledge and skills to give Azithromycin to eligible children during the campaign.
Understand proper dosing and schedules for AZM, and know when to refer a child to a health facility.
Learn safeguarding practices that protect children and vulnerable people during AZM drug administration.
Learn good interpersonal communication to teach caregivers about AZM and its possible side effects.
Practise every part of AZM drug administration through demonstration and role plays.

content.text: Acronyms

rows: State primary health care Development Agency

content.caption: In the field — CDDs in AZM vests speak with a family before giving AZM.
content.alt: Two community drug distributors in yellow AZM vests talk with a seated man and woman holding a child. A baby crawls on a mat. Thatched huts are behind them.

content.text: What is AZM?
AZM means Azithromycin.
AZM POS means Azithromycin Powdered Oral Suspension.
AZM benefits

items: Azithromycin is a broad-spectrum antibiotic.
It prevents and treats many bacterial infections: acute lower respiratory tract, skin and soft tissue, and gastro-enteric infections.
It also protects against malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum.
It reduces childhood deaths by preventing and treating pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria.

content.text: Who receives AZM?
AZM drug administration protects children aged 1-59 months from childhood infections.
AZM is given every six months (bi-annually) to children 1 to 59 months of age.
How is AZM delivered?

items: Trained Community Drug Distributors (CDDs) go door to door.
CDD supervisors, LGA, State and National teams supervise them.
CDDs record AZM administration in the DIGIT HCM app on their devices.

content.text: Delivery platforms
AZM MDA uses these child health interventions:

items: Neglected tropical disease (NTDs).
Polio Eradication Initiative campaign.
Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention.
Maternal Newborn and Child health (MNCH).

content.text: Using these platforms reduces costs, makes the most of resources and reaches more eligible children.
Tools for each participant

items: AZM Job Aid.
Sample of AZM POS.
DIGIT HCM App.

title: Eligibility for AZM
description: Which children can receive AZM, how to estimate age, and who must not receive it.

content.caption: In the field — a CDD shows the AZM pack to a mother and her children.
content.alt: A woman CDD in an orange headscarf and yellow vest holds out a small AZM box to a seated mother with a baby and a girl in a yellow dress.

content.text: Age eligibility

items: AZM is given only to healthy children between 1 to 59 months of age.
Children less than one month or older than 59 months are not eligible.
Neonates (less than one month) are not eligible.
A child who is 59 months in round one receives AZM, but is not eligible in the next round.

content.text: Why only children 1 to 59 months?

items: The AZM safety protocol was set for children 1 month and above.
Younger children are more likely to have side effects.
Children 1 to 59 months have the highest risk of severe malaria and other childhood infections.
This age group has the highest death rates from childhood infections.
Side effects are easier to monitor in this age group (1-59 months).

content.text: How to find the child's age

items: Ask to see the child's health card.
Ask the caregiver the age of the child.
Use a calendar of events.

content.caption: Step — use these signs to estimate the age of a child under 12 months.
content.alt: Four drawings under the label Children 1 to 11 months: a sleeping baby (1 to 2 months), a newborn crossed out in red, a baby held sitting (3 to 4 months), and a crawling baby and a sitting girl (5 to 11 months).

items: 1 to 2 months: cannot hold head and neck steady when held upright.
Newborn, less than one month: not eligible (marked with a red X).
3 to 4 months: can hold head and neck steady when held upright.
5 to 11 months: can crawl and can sit without help.

content.text: From 3 to 11 months, a child can hold head and neck steady, crawl, and sit without help.

content.caption: Step — a child of 12 to 59 months can stand or walk, but cannot do the two tests marked X.
content.alt: Drawings under the label Child 12 to 59 months: two children standing and walking, a boy trying to touch his opposite ear over his head with a red X, and a boy standing on one foot with a red X.

items: Can stand, walk or run.
CANNOT raise the arm over the head and touch the opposite ear.
CANNOT stand or jump on one foot.

content.heading: Older than 59 months: not eligible
content.text: A child older than 59 months can raise the arm and touch the opposite ear. They can stand on one leg for 10 secs or jump on one leg. Do not give AZM.
Eligible and not eligible

content.caption: Do give AZM to healthy children aged 1 to 59 months, like those shown here.
content.alt: A green tick next to drawings of healthy children: a sleeping baby, a baby held sitting, a crawling baby, a girl eating and a standing boy.

content.caption: Do not give AZM to a child with any of these signs. Refer the child.
content.alt: A red X next to five line drawings labelled Difficulty in swallowing, Severe acute malnutrition, Not eating and Very Sick. The fifth drawing, a child holding the forehead, has no label.

sections.title: Not eligible: signs in the picture

items: Difficulty in swallowing.
Severe acute malnutrition.
Not eating.
Very sick.
Fifth picture: child holding the forehead (no label in the flipbook).

sections.title: Do not give AZM to sick children or children with SAM

content.heading: Do not give AZM to sick children or children with SAM
content.text: Do NOT give AZM to children who are sick or who have Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM).

items: Advise the caregiver to take the child to the nearest health facility for further evaluation.
Complete the referral form and give it to the caregiver to take to the health facility.

sections.title: Do not hand over medicine or the card

content.heading: Do not hand over medicine or the card
content.text: Do not give the caregiver the AZM medicine to give later, or the child record card.

sections.title: Do not give AZM to children with allergy

content.heading: Do not give AZM to children with allergy
content.text: Do NOT give AZM to children who are allergic to AZM or other macrolide antibiotics.

items: Does the child get sick after taking antibiotic medicines or similar medications?
Has the child taken AZM or similar antibiotics before?
If so, did the child get sick or have reactions such as rashes, swelling or difficulty breathing?

sections.title: Do not give AZM after recent antibiotics

content.heading: Do not give AZM after recent antibiotics
content.text: Do not give AZM after antibiotics or similar medicine taken in the last 28 days (4 weeks).

items: Has the child taken any medicine in the last 28 days or 4 weeks?
If yes, what medicine has the child taken in the past one month?
If possible, ask to see the packet to confirm.

content.text: Severe acute malnutrition: look and feel

items: Visible severe wasting: the child looks extremely thin.
The ribs, shoulder blades and bones are very prominent.
The arms and thighs look like "skin and bones", with little or no muscle.
The child's buttocks may look flat or baggy.
Press gently with your thumb on the top of both feet for about 3 seconds.
If a pit remains after you remove the thumb, oedema is present.
This shows the child has Kwashiorkor, a form of SAM.

content.text: AZM should not be given to these children

items: Children from 60 months and older.
Children allergic to AZM or similar antibiotics.
Children who are sick or have fever.
Children who received AZM or other antibiotics in the last one month.
Children who are currently taking AZM or other antibiotics.
Children who cannot swallow.

content.caption: Step — check each row: only a healthy child of 1 to 59 months is eligible.
content.alt: A chart with Eligible and Refer columns. A green tick for children 1 to 59 months. Red X and refer ticks for a sick child, fever, and allergy or malnutrition. A red X with no referral for AZM in the last 28 days.

title: Referral of Children to the Health Facility
description: When to refer a child, signs of allergy, and the referral steps.

content.caption: In the field — a CDD explains a referral to a caregiver, holding the referral form.
content.alt: A man in a yellow AZM vest points down the road and holds a paper while talking to a woman carrying a toddler. A second CDD in a vest stands beside her.

content.text: When to refer a sick child
A child is sick or has danger signs when the child has:

items: Convulsion.
Fever or high temperature.
Difficulty breathing.
Difficulty staying awake.
Vomiting.
Not able to eat or drink.
Severe pains or bleeding.
Neck pain or severe headache.
Severe Acute Malnutrition.

content.caption: Do refer the child when the child is sick or has danger signs.
content.alt: A green tick beside a drawing of a mother holding a sick child, with the labels When the child is sick and When the child has danger signs.

content.caption: Do refer the child when the child has fever.
content.alt: A green tick beside a drawing of a child holding the forehead, with the label When the child has fever.

content.text: Why refer?

items: Children with fever may have malaria or other childhood infections.
Malaria, pneumonia and diarrhoea are the leading causes of death in under-five children in Nigeria.
Children with fever need evaluation to avoid complications.
Children with SAM after MUAC screening are excluded, evaluated and given support (resuscitation, feeding programme, etc.).

content.text: Allergy and side effects
Allergies to AZM are rare but may occur.
Refer a child to the nearest health facility if the child has side effects or suspected adverse reactions.

content.caption: Do refer a child who shows any of these signs after AZM.
content.alt: Four drawings labelled Very Sick (mother holding a child), Fever (child holding forehead), Swelling (child with swollen face) and Rash (child with a red rash on the chest).

content.caption: Do not give AZM to a child with any of these signs. Refer the child.
content.alt: Five line drawings labelled Difficulty in swallowing, Severe acute malnutrition, Not eating, Very Sick and Fever.

sections.title: Possible allergy or reasons for exclusion

items: Swelling of the face, mouth, tongue or other parts of the body.
Nausea or continuous vomiting.
Skin rashes or blistering of the skin.
Body itching.
Weakness or fatigue.
Loss of appetite.
Abdominal pains, diarrhoea.
Headache.
Yellowing of the skin or eyes.

content.text: Referral steps
Use these steps for children who are sick, have severe acute malnutrition or have suspected adverse reactions.

content.caption: Step — do not give AZM, fill the referral form, then explain the referral to the caregiver.
content.alt: Three pictures joined by green arrows: a red X over a photo of suspension poured into a cup (Do Not give AZM), a health worker writing on a form (Fill referral form), and a health worker showing the form to a seated woman (Explain referral to caregiver).

items: Do not give AZM.
Complete the top portion of the referral form.
Explain the reason for the referral and the need to act immediately.
Tell the caregiver how to get to the nearest health facility.
Give the AZM referral form to the caregiver to take to the health facility.

content.heading: Explain the danger
content.text: If the child has fever or SAM, the child could have malaria or other diseases. Explain that the child could get worse or die without immediate treatment.
Explain that the health worker will evaluate the child at the facility.

content.heading: Key take away of module 3
content.text: 1. Refer children who are sick or malnourished to the nearest health facility. 2. Fill out the referral form and give it to the caregiver to take to the health facility. 3. Explain the reason for referral and encourage the caregiver to take the child to the health facility immediately.

title: Giving AZM Safely
description: Preparing AZM POS, dosing by age and height, giving the dose and observing the child.

content.caption: Step — the caregiver gives AZM slowly from the dispensing cup while the child sits upright.
content.alt: Photo of a woman in a teal headscarf holding a small plastic cup to the lips of a young boy sitting on her lap.

content.text: AZM Powdered Oral Suspension (AZM POS)

items: AZM comes in a small bottle of powdered oral suspension (POS).
It comes with a small dispensing cup to measure an accurate dose.
Reconstitute it with 15ml of clean water to obtain 30ml AZM suspension.
Each bottle of AZM is used to reach 4 children.

content.caption: Step — check expiry, wash hands, get clean water, reconstitute, then measure the dose.
content.alt: Five numbered pictures in a row: 1 a bottle labelled Expiry Date, 2 hands washed under a tap, 3 a measuring jug of water, 4 a CDD in a vest holding a bottle with a family, 5 white suspension poured into a cup.

sections.title: Steps in the picture (transcribed from image)

items: Check the expiry date of the medicine.
Wash hands.
Provide clean water from the household.
Reconstitute AZM medicine.
Measure out AZM for dispensing.

content.text: Safe AZM administration

items: Check the expiry date of the drug before reconstitution.
Wash hands with soap and water before giving AZM.
Limit AZM administration to 5 eligible children at a time.
Ask the caregiver to bring drinking water in a small cup.

content.heading: Do not use expired AZM
content.text: Check the expiry date of the AZM POS before administration. Do not use it if it has expired.
Mixing AZM POS

items: Azithromycin POS.
Safe drinking water in a clean cup.
A calibrated measuring cup.
Shake or tap the bottle to loosen the dry powder.
Measure and add 15ml of water to obtain 30ml final volume of AZM suspension.
Use the provided measuring cup to add the correct amount of water.
Close the bottle tightly and shake well for at least 30 secs, until the powder fully dissolves.
Shake again before each use.

content.text: Dose by age and height

items: For children 12-59 months, measure height with the dosing pole (height-based dosing).
The pole shows height in cm on one side and the matching dose on the other side.
The DIGIT HCM app shows the dose when you enter the child's age or height.
Measure the exact dose with the provided dispensing cup.

content.text: Giving AZM

items: Ensure the child is awake.
Sit the child upright to avoid spitting or vomiting.
Give the medicine slowly with the dispensing cup.
Rinse the cup with a little water and give it, so the child drinks ALL the medicine.
Give AZM to one child at a time.

content.heading: Do not force the child
content.text: Do not force the child to swallow by holding the head and neck backwards or pinching the nose.

items: If the child vomits within 5 minutes, redose with the same dose for the age or height.
Observe the child for 30 minutes after administration for any side effect or suspected ADR.
Refer any child with a side effect or suspected ADR.

content.text: How AZM is issued and returned

items: OICs in the facilities issue AZM and other tools to each CDD team at the start of each day.
CDD teams meet the OIC every morning to request the AZM they need.
Each CDD team should reach a total of 100 children each day, over the 4 days distribution period.

sections.title: Returned to the OIC at the end of each day

items: All AZM bottles must be accounted for daily during the MDA.
All used and unused bottles must be returned to the health facility OIC.
Partially used AZM stays viable for up to 2 to 3 days. Use it before opening a new bottle.
CDDs must return the dosing poles to the health facility daily.

content.heading: Measure the exact dose
content.text: Measure the exact dose shown in the DIGIT app. Overdosing or underdosing wastes drug, causes accountability issues and drug resistance.

items: The OIC checks the technology app for the number of children reached by each CDD team.
The OIC documents AZM distribution in the inventory control cards.
All empty bottles are arranged in the cartons.

title: Drug Safety and Side Effects
description: Side effects, adverse events and serious adverse events, and why they are reported.

content.caption: Possible side effects — watch children after AZM and refer any child who becomes unwell.
content.alt: Six drawn panels: a sad child sitting by a puddle, a man holding a crying baby, a girl in bed offered water, a child on a bed given a cup, a girl kneeling and holding her stomach near a latrine, and a woman holding her stomach in pain.

content.text: Drug safety during AZM
Drug safety means monitoring and managing the risks of medicines, so the benefits outweigh any harm.

rows: Minor, expected reactions to medicines that do not require stopping treatment.
Any untoward medical occurrence at any dose resulting in death, hospitalization or longer hospitalization, persistent or significant disability or incapacity, or congenital anomaly or birth defect.

content.heading: Report serious adverse events immediately
content.text: Serious adverse events must be reported immediately.

items: Pharmacovigilance aims at rational and safe use of medicines.
It assesses and communicates the risks and benefits of medicines, to improve patient care and public health.
No drug is always safe for everyone.
Know the possible side effects, monitor children, and refer them immediately to the health facility.

title: Interpersonal Communication and SBC
description: Good communication with caregivers and the SBC methods used in the AZM campaign.

content.caption: Do talk with caregivers respectfully and explain AZM clearly.
content.alt: Photo of a woman CDD in an orange headscarf and yellow vest gesturing as she talks with a seated mother holding a baby and a standing girl in a yellow dress.

content.text: Why interpersonal communication matters

items: Good communication builds trust and helps make sure AZM is given safely.
Respect the cultural norms of the community.
Greet the head of household and caregivers with respect, and recognize the child.
Use words they will understand, and use the pictures in the AZM job aid.
Use open-ended questions to get more information.
Listen carefully to what the head of household or caregiver says.
Give time to answer, and show you are listening by nodding or saying "I understand".
Stop from time to time to ask if they understand or have any questions.
Ask the caregiver to repeat the information about AZM.
Ask questions that get the answers you need.
Let others share information without interruption.
Explain health messages so they are understood.
Protects children from pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria.
Prevents and treats other bacterial infections.

rows: Closed-ended: gets a yes or no answer
Is your child between 1 to 59 months? Is your child sick today? Did you have any problems with the last round of AZM?
How old is your child? How is your child feeling today? How did your child feel after the last round of AZM?

content.text: Social and behaviour change (SBC)
SBC is a strategic approach that influences behaviour by engaging communities through tailored messages.

sections.title: SBC methods in the AZM campaign

items: Interpersonal communication.
Mass media campaigns.
Community mobilization.
Visual aids.
Ask participants which SBC tools for AZM MDA they have seen or used.
Show examples of AZM job aids, posters and banners used in the community.

title: Safeguarding
description: Protecting children and vulnerable adults during the AZM campaign, and reporting concerns.

content.caption: Do give AZM from the cup while the child sits upright. Do not force medicine into a lying child's mouth.
content.alt: Three photos. A mother gives a seated boy medicine from a cup. A green tick over a girl drinking from a cup among children and caregivers. A red X over an adult forcing liquid from a spoon into a lying baby's mouth.

content.text: What safeguarding means

items: Safeguarding is an organization's commitment that staff and activities do not harm children and vulnerable adults.
It means not exposing them to abuse, harm, risk or exploitation.
It protects the rights and dignity of all, especially children and vulnerable adults.
Respectful interaction with caregivers and their families.
Educating community members on the benefits of AZM.
Addressing caregivers' concerns about the AZM campaign.
Ensuring informed consent from caregivers.
Handling AZM medicines safely during the campaign.

content.text: Protection during the AZM campaign
Protection means taking action when children or vulnerable people are at risk or experience harm.

items: Ensure only eligible children receive AZM.
Give the correct dose.
Prevent overdosing during MDA.
Refer sick children to the nearest health facility.

content.text: Safeguarding during the campaign

items: Select CDDs with active community involvement, so they represent the community and act with integrity.
Caregivers have the right to informed consent, dignity and respect. They can know the names of the CDD and supervisors.
Give caregivers complete, accurate information, including risks and what to do after an adverse reaction.
Caregivers need a way to get support or raise concerns and complaints.
The consent form should list a few designated contacts they can reach.

content.heading: Never force AZM
content.text: CDDs must not force AZM on caregivers or treat children harshly.

content.caption: Do not take pictures without consent.
content.alt: Photo of a man holding a camera to his face, with a large red X over it.

content.caption: Do not take pictures without consent, including with a phone.
content.alt: Photo of a person holding up a smartphone to take a picture in a dry field, with a large red X over it.

content.caption: Do not take or give bribes. Avoid all corrupt practices, sexual harassment and exploitation.
content.alt: Close-up photo of hands holding a bundle of Nigerian 1000 naira notes, with a large red X over it.

content.heading: Avoid corrupt practices
content.text: Avoid bribery and all forms of corrupt practices in the field, including sexual harassment and exploitation.
Reporting safeguarding issues

items: Report all safeguarding issues to the CDD supervisor or health facility OIC.
They escalate it to the NTD coordinator of the LGA team and partners.
Report any case or suspected case of violence or neglect of eligible children to the health facility OIC.
The OIC escalates it to Malaria Consortium through the appropriate MoH structures.

content.heading: Report safeguarding issues
content.text: Report all safeguarding issues to concenrns@malariaconsortium.org.

title: MUAC Nutrition Assessment
description: Measuring MUAC on children 6-59 months and acting on the result.

content.text: MUAC nutrition assessment (children 6–59 months)

items: MUAC is done during routine SARMAAN II household visits.
It uses trained CDDs and existing supervision structures.
Data is collected on the Kobo Collect digital platform.
It uses existing household engagement processes.
No extra household visits are needed.
Measure the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) with a standard colour-coded MUAC tape.
Use the left arm.
Find the correct midpoint.
Apply the tape lightly or comfortably.

sections.title: Do not pull the tape tight

content.heading: Do not pull the tape tight
content.text: The MUAC tape must not be tight or too tight.
Kobo Collect classifies MUAC values automatically using WHO/UNICEF thresholds.

content.caption: Step — read the MUAC result and take the action in the same row.
content.alt: A colour-coded table: green row 12.5 cm or more, yellow row 11.5 to 12.4 cm, pink row less than 11.5 cm, with status, classification and action columns.

rows: Immediate referral to health facility for counselling

content.caption: Do measure on the left arm, not too tight. Do not use the right arm or pull the tape too tight.
content.alt: Two illustrated panels. Green panel, Good MUAC assessment: a CDD measures a girl's left arm, labels Left arm and Not too tight. Red panel, Bad MUAC assessment: a CDD measures a child's right arm, labels Right arm and Too tight.

sections.title: MUAC right and wrong (transcribed from image)

items: Good: left arm.
Good: not too tight.
Bad: right arm.
Bad: too tight.

content.caption: Step — wrap the MUAC tape around the upper arm of a child aged 6-59 months.
content.alt: Close-up photo of adult hands wrapping a green and red MUAC tape around a child's upper arm. The child wears a striped shirt.

content.caption: The MUAC tape: red from 6 to 11 cm, yellow at 12 cm, green from 13 to 26 cm.
content.alt: Technical drawing of a MUAC tape with a UNICEF logo, a cm window and a scale from 6 to 26 with red, yellow and green bands. Small dimension labels are not readable.

title: Drug Accountability and Reconciliation
description: Issuing, counting, reconciling, storing and returning AZM bottles at the health facility.

content.text: Drug accountability and reconciliation in the health facility

content.caption: Step — count and arrange AZM bottles in cartons for accountability.
content.alt: Photo of several people bending over open cardboard cartons, taking out and sorting white AZM bottles.

items: OICs document AZM bottles received using the Issue and Receipt Voucher and the Inventory Control Card.
OICs issue the bottles each CDD team needs for its daily target, physically and in the technology app.
The number of bottles issued in the app must match the physical bottles issued.
All physical quantities issued to each CDD team are documented in the Inventory Control Card.
Keep AZM bottles safely in the AZM bags provided, to avoid losses.
Reconstitute each bottle with exactly 15 ml of water.
Measure the exact dose shown on the app with the calibrated cups.
Capture any redosing for vomiting within 5 minutes in the app.
Finish each opened bottle before opening another.
CDD teams separate empty bottles from unopened or unused bottles in the AZM bag.
The OIC counts each team's empty bottles and multiplies by 4. This gives the number of children to be reached.
The OIC compares this number with the children reached in the DIGIT HCM app.
Unopened plus empty bottles returned must equal the bottles issued that morning.
Arrange empty and unopened bottles in separate cartons in the health facility.
Escalate all missing bottles to the LGA logistician and the NTD coordinator for investigation.
Return all AZM bottles (used and unused) in cartons to the LGA store within 3 days after implementation.

content.heading: Key take away: drug accountability
content.text: CDD teams and OICs are responsible for AZM accountability at the health facility. Lack of accountability leads to pilferage and diversion of drugs into markets and drug sales outlets. Reconcile AZM and other commodities daily, at the end of the day. Arrange all used and unused bottles in cartons.

content.text: What supervision is
Supervision is coordinated oversight of drug administration, logistics, data collection and community engagement. It makes sure all activities run effectively and efficiently.

items: Accurate administration of AZM.
Compliance with safety protocols and timely reporting of adverse drug reactions.
Supply chain monitoring to prevent stock-outs and wastage.

On-the-job mentoring and training for CDDs and health facility workers.
Community engagement to build caregiver compliance and trust.
Conduct daily field visits to monitor drug administration and community engagement.
Verify real-time recording of drug administration by CDDs in DIGIT HCM.
Complete and submit supervision checklists with the e-checklist.
Check adherence to dosage protocols and safety measures.
Identify and resolve logistical and operational challenges in real time.
Work closely with the LGA and community stakeholders to improve implementation.
Attend review meetings and escalate challenges.
Provide immediate feedback.

rows: Ensure supervisory plans are followed, logistics are coordinated and CDDs are supported. Monitor daily operations, distribution and community sensitization. Conduct field visits and submit structured supervision checklists.
Support CDDs in drug administration, record keeping and referral of suspected adverse reactions. Ensure pharmacovigilance measures are in place. Review DIGIT HCM entries for data accuracy.
Provide high-level coordination, policy guidance and overall campaign evaluation. Use administrative and supervision data for drug administration tracking and supervisory analysis.
